Silesia
sy-LEE-zha
n. (the cluster of duchies north-east of Bohemia, Lutheran from the 1520s, and the land of the churches of peace and of grace)
Latin Silesia, German Schlesien, Polish Śląsk, from the river Slza or the Silingi who are said to have dwelt about Mount Zobten.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Silesia was a patchwork of duchies under the Bohemian crown, mostly German-speaking, and it took the Reformation faster and held it longer than any other Habsburg land. Breslau heard Lutheran preaching in 1518, and Frederick II of Legnica carried his duchy over in 1522 and founded a short-lived evangelical university at Liegnitz in 1526. Most of the duchies followed, and by 1600 Silesia was overwhelmingly Lutheran with Reformed and Schwenckfeldian minorities, Caspar Schwenckfeld himself being a Silesian nobleman whose spiritualising of the sacraments the Lutherans rejected. The Habsburg recovery after 1620 closed hundreds of churches, but Silesia was never fully recatholicised: the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 allowed three churches of peace, to be built outside the town walls of Glogau, Jauer and Schweidnitz of wood, clay and straw with no tower and no bell, and the Convention of Altranstadt in 1707, forced on the emperor by Charles XII of Sweden, allowed six more churches of grace. The dictionary enters Silesia because those timber churches, built to humiliating specifications and filled for generations, are the most exact picture in European history of a church permitted to exist on condition that it look like nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a duchy as the territory of a duke; a convention as an assembly or an agreement; grace as the free unmerited favour of God; and a tower as a lofty building of several stories.

expand to see more

DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.

CONVENTION, n. The act of coming together; an assembly; also, an agreement or contract between parties.

GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart.

TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation and consisting of several stories.

TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture and the like.

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Isa 1:9 — "Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah."

Modern Corruption

Duchies under the Bohemian crown, Lutheran from 1522, never fully recatholicised, and granted the timber churches of peace in 1648 and of grace in 1707.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the toleration that is really a humiliation, and Silesia is where it can be seen in its measurements. The churches of peace might be built of wood, clay and straw only, outside the walls, within a year, at the congregation's own cost, with no tower, no bell and no stone; the terms were written to make the Lutheran church of a Lutheran country look like a barn on sufferance. The congregations built them anyway, at Schweidnitz to hold seven thousand, and filled them for two centuries, which is the right answer to a humiliating permission.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's dignity is not in its fabric and its security is not in its charter. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) was spoken to a congregation with no building at all. Silesia also shows the mercy that keeps a remnant where a settlement fails: “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) is the Silesian case, for the three churches were a very small remnant of some fifteen hundred that had been taken away, and they were enough.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sarid (H8300), a survivor, a remnant; Greek stephanos (G4735), a crown, a victor's garland; Greek exousia (G1849), authority.

expand to see more

Greek stephanos (G4735) — a crown, the garland given a victor; “I will give thee a crown of life”, Revelation 2:10.

Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “be thou faithful unto death”, Revelation 2:10.

Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, one left over; “a very small remnant”, Isaiah 1:9.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, delegated power; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Hebrew ani (H6041) — afflicted, poor, bowed down; “an afflicted and poor people”, Zephaniah 3:12.

Usage

"“be thou faithful unto death” (Rev 2:10) — the churches of peace at Glogau, Jauer and Schweidnitz, 1648."

"“a very small remnant” (Isa 1:9) — three churches permitted where fifteen hundred had been closed."

"“an afflicted and poor people” (Zep 3:12) — timber, clay and straw, no tower and no bell."
